items.title: Association Between Repetitive Movement Exposure and Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Symptoms Among Office Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Purpose: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) symptoms are an occupational health concern among office workers who perform repetitive hand and wrist movements during computer-based activities. This study aimed to examine the association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptoms among office workers at PT Karya Bintang Mandiri. Materials and Methods: This analytical cross-sectional study involved 164 office workers recruited using purposive sampling. Repetitive movement exposure was assessed using the Occupational Repetitive Actions (OCRA) Checklist, while CTS symptoms were evaluated using the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTQ). Descriptive statistics and the Pearson Chi-Square test were used to examine the association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptoms. Result: Moderate repetitive movement exposure was observed in 83 participants (50.6%), followed by high exposure in 42 (25.6%) and low exposure in 39 (23.8%). Regarding CTS symptoms, 62 participants (37.8%) reported no symptoms, 68 (41.5%) reported mild symptoms, 32 (19.5%) reported moderate symptoms, and 2 (1.2%) reported severe symptoms. The Pearson Chi-Square test indicated a significant association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptom categories, χ²(6) = 35.06, p < 0.001. In a supplementary dichotomized analysis, the prevalence of moderate-to-severe CTS symptoms was 47.6% (20/42) among workers with high exposure and 11.5% (14/122) among workers with low-to-moderate exposure (prevalence ratio [PR] = 4.15; 95% CI: 2.31–7.46). Conclusion: Repetitive movement exposure was associated with CTS symptom categories among office workers at PT Karya Bintang Mandiri. These findings support the importance of ergonomic risk assessment and preventive measures in office environments. Further studies using longitudinal designs and clinical diagnostic assessments are warranted.

items.title: ASTRA: An Autonomous Framework for Physics-Validated Analysis and Hypothesis Generation in Astrophysics
items.abstract: Abstract We present ASTRA, an autonomous framework for physics-validated analysis and hypothesis generation in astrophysics without per-step human intervention. It integrates dimensional analysis, structural causal models, Bayesian evidence computation, and multi-wavelength data fusion in a single automated workflow. Five test cases on real observational data recover known results: Herschel filament scaling, Chandra Deep Field South cross-matching, SDSS galaxy correlations, Gaia causal inference, and Bayesian virial model selection. A sixth case runs unsupervised on synthetic galaxy data: the main sequence and mass–metallicity relation are recovered, and the outlier detector, with a false-discovery-rate threshold and no contamination parameter, recovers the blind injected fraction on ten sealed datasets (purity >0.99) and flags nothing on the 3,000-galaxy sample. A knowledge-isolation ablation shows pattern detection and physical validation are invariant to removal of domain knowledge, which affects only interpretation. In a direct comparison, agentic-LLM and pure-ML baselines match the statistical fitting but not the physics-validation stage: they rarely derive the equilibrium benchmark, split evenly on the physical verdict, and adopt a supplied erroneous benchmark in all six trap runs; an astrophysics-specific fine-tuned model completes zero of six runs. On live SDSS DR16 data it flags 197 of 4,999 galaxies at a data-determined threshold, ranked extremes classifiable from withheld spectroscopy. These are recovery validations and capability demonstrations rather than discoveries, with hypothesis generation demonstrated qualitatively.

items.title: AudioRSI: Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

items.title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
items.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

items.title: Autonomous hardware security evaluation from reconnaissance to physical validation
items.abstract: Abstract Physical hardware-security evaluation requires both target-specific reasoning and control of laboratory instruments. This study presents a large language model (LLM) agent that links reconnaissance, vulnerability hypotheses, laser fault-injection experiments and reporting through human approval gates. The agent reverse-engineers firmware and instruction behaviour, combines this evidence with documentation and chip imagery, and generates bounded experiments with predefined rules for classifying outcomes. On an ATmega328P microcontroller, agent-derived experiments produced a skipped processor load instruction, acceptance of an incorrect personal identification number (PIN), and the same two-byte Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) encrypted-output difference in 14 trials, with 29 paired fault-free controls. Photon-emission imaging narrowed the physical search region. A second campaign on an Artix-7 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) tested transfer to programmable logic using firmware-binary analysis, optical-to-layout registration and cryptographic-output classification. Recorded agent and operator decisions connect observations to experimental revisions and documented conclusions, demonstrating an autonomous workflow across two hardware architectures.

items.title: AutoRSE: Evaluating LLM Agents as Recommendation Engineers for Self-Evolving Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Recommender Systems Engineer Agents (RSE-Agents), which use LLM-based agents to autonomously improve recommendation algorithms, are emerging as a promising paradigm. However, their capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood due to the lack of a unified, standardized evaluation framework and systematic trajectory-level analysis. To address this gap, we introduce AutoRSE, an evaluation framework spanning six representative industrial-grade recommendation tasks, and conduct a large-scale empirical study of three frontier LLMs across three widely used agent harnesses. Our results show that RSE-Agents consistently enhance the performance of backbones on five of the six tasks, with an average relative improvement of 16.1%, indicating that they can already autonomously improve recommendation performance. However, trajectory-level analysis also reveals that current RSE-Agents function primarily as engineering optimizers rather than algorithmic improvers: their gains are largely driven by hyperparameter tuning, training strategies, and model ensembling, while genuine algorithmic innovations are rare. Since the largest gains in recommender systems often stem from algorithmic advances, this behavior underscores a fundamental limitation of current RSE-Agents. To probe this limitation, we perform idea-injection experiments and show that agents equipped with innovative ideas from frontier research or human experts achieve substantially larger improvements than those relying on self-generated ideas. These results suggest that idea generation is a central bottleneck of current RSE-Agents, highlights a key direction for the future recommendation system research. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/Ray-Tiann/AutoRSE.

items.title: Balancing Cultural Preservation and Design: A Study on the Generative Artificial Intelligence-Empowered Framework for the Sustainable Design of Intangible Cultural Heritage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is a form of AI technology that can automatically generate new content, such as text, images, and audio, based on prompts. This study explores the opportunities and structural challenges of using Gen-AI to promote sustainable design in the field of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) from the perspectives of ICH designers and relevant experts. The research employed a variety of methods, including interviews (n= 40), grounded theory, the Delphi method (n = 20), exploratory factor analysis (n = 312), confirmatory factor analysis (n = 324), and expert interviews (n = 10). The study evaluated deep-seated issues arising from Gen-AI’s intervention in ICH design practices, such as cultural subjectivity, knowledge, power relations, and value circulation, through the lenses of Cultural Ecology, Extraction of Intangible Cultural Heritage Genes, Sustainable Communication, Technology Generation, and Human–Machine Collaborative Design. The results suggest that Gen-AI’s empowerment involves a tension between technological generative capabilities and cultural accuracy, as well as systemic-level transformations such as balancing communication efficiency with cultural depth and human–machine collaboration, and re-configuring the designer’s role.

items.title: Barriers and Facilitators to Accessing Musculoskeletal Disorders (Msd) Treatment and Care Services Among Casual Workers at Construction Sites in Kampala Metropolitan Area, Uganda: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are common among construction workers because of physically demanding, repetitive work and heavy lifting. Casual construction workers may face additional challenges to care due to financial insecurity, limited occupational health protections, and the temporary nature of their employment. This study describes the work-related exposures that casual construction workers attributed to their MSD symptoms, and the barriers and facilitators to accessing MSD treatment and care services, in the Kampala Metropolitan Area (KMA), Uganda. Methods A qualitative descriptive study, framed by an interpretivist perspective and a constructionist epistemological position, was conducted among 15 casual construction workers and 10 key informants in KMA. Participants were selected using purposive and snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews (IDIs) with casual workers and key informant interviews (KIIs) with stakeholders involved in occupational safety and health, labour administration, and construction-site management. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and translated where necessary. Data were analyzed thematically using ATLAS.ti 7.5, combining deductive and inductive coding. Reporting follows the COREQ checklist. Results Participants attributed MSD symptoms to heavy lifting, repetitive tasks, prolonged working hours, inadequate rest, poor ergonomics, and limited safety equipment and training. Barriers to accessing care included limited awareness of MSD services and occupational health rights, financial constraints, employment insecurity, inadequate employer support, limited MSD-specific training, complex compensation procedures, weak OSH implementation, and limited access to specialized occupational health services. Workers often delayed care, continued working despite pain, or self-medicated when treatment seemed costly or risked income or job loss. Facilitators included employer support (sick leave, safety programmes, OSH inspections, health assessments, first aid, on-site healthcare, referral linkages, compensation mechanisms, OSH personnel) and social support, but were more consistently available in larger, better-resourced projects. Conclusion Access to MSD care among casual construction workers is shaped by interconnected individual, economic, workplace, and health-system factors. Strengthening worker education, enforcing OSH requirements, improving affordable occupational health services, compensation mechanisms, and workplace support could promote earlier MSD reporting and treatment. Findings reflect 25 participants recruited in one metropolitan area and are not statistically representative.

items.title: BenchMeUp: Building Software Engineering Benchmarks from Natural-Language Specifications
items.abstract: Software-engineering research relies on benchmarks that evaluate new techniques on a set of problem instances. Unfortunately, manually constructing benchmarks is labor-intensive, as researchers must find suitable instances, prepare execution environments, establish expected outcomes, and validate correctness. This paper presents BenchMeUp, an approach for automatically creating software-engineering benchmarks from natural-language specifications. Given a specification defining the desired instances, data sources, and evaluation procedures, BenchMeUp generates search rules and a construction plan, invokes parallel LLM agents that identify candidate instances and construct executable instances, validates the results in fresh execution environments, and packages the instances behind a unified command-line interface. We evaluate the approach on four tasks: program repair, issue reproduction, compiler autotuning, and fixing static-analysis warnings. Targeting 50 instances per task (200 in total), BenchMeUp constructs 198 instances, of which 196 (99\%) are successfully packaged. Search and construction take 36 minutes and \$0.79 per instance, on average. Evaluating eight existing techniques on the generated benchmarks, we find that 189 of 196 packaged instances (96\%) support end-to-end evaluation, allowing users to study the effectiveness of the techniques. Checking every constructed instance against its source, the specification, and its expected outcome, we find that 180 of 198 (91\%) meet all criteria, compared with 10 of 200 instances delivered by Codex (general-purpose coding agent). Overall, we show that LLM-based agents can automate benchmark construction across diverse software-engineering tasks and produce executable instances that existing techniques can use, while validity beyond execution still needs to be checked.

items.title: Between tradition and algorithm: Human–AI co-creation in textile design education and its implications for cultural authenticity
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of generative AI into creative industries has intensified debates about the future of culturally grounded design practice. This study examines how three production conditions (human-only, AI-assisted, and fully autonomous AI) differentially affect the perceived cultural fidelity, creativity, aesthetics, and commercial viability of textile designs rooted in traditional Anatolian kilim motifs, a question with limited prior empirical evidence in design education. Using a within-subjects design, fifteen undergraduate textile design students produced designs under each condition, using a generative AI platform with substantial commercial reach in the Turkish textile sector for the AI-involved conditions. A panel of ten expert evaluators, five academics and five industry designers, rated 45 designs against a seven-criterion rubric under blind conditions. Cultural fidelity, creativity, originality, and aesthetics differed significantly across conditions (all p < .05). Both human-only and AI-assisted designs preserved cultural fidelity at equivalent levels, and both significantly exceeded fully autonomous AI outputs. Paradoxically, fully autonomous AI outputs received the highest scores for creativity and originality, pointing to a trade-off between perceived novelty and cultural coherence. No significant differences emerged for commercial viability, technical feasibility, or compositional integrity, indicating parity across production methods on industrially relevant dimensions. Academic and industry evaluators converged on cultural fidelity judgements while diverging on more subjective aesthetic criteria. These findings suggest that human involvement acts as a cultural filter that cannot be replicated through textual instruction alone, and that even minimal human intervention, selecting and lightly editing AI-generated variants, is sufficient to preserve culturally identifiable design characteristics. The results have implications for textile design pedagogy, for AI governance in heritage-sensitive industries, and for theorising human–AI co-creation in cultural production contexts.

items.title: Beyond Knowledge Transfer: the Multi-Faceted Role of Islamic Religious Education Teachers in Catalyzing Student Motivation
items.abstract: Students’ learning motivation is an important factor in effective learning, while Islamic Religious Education teachers have a strategic role in fostering motivation through pedagogical, motivational, and exemplary practices. This study aims to describe the planning and implementation of Islamic Religious Education teachers’ efforts to enhance students’ learning motivation and to analyze their outcomes in terms of student engagement, subject comprehension, religious attitudes, and character development. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design conducted at MTs Wahid Hasyim Dau Malang. The research subjects and data sources included 2 (two) Islamic Religious Education teachers, and 2 (two) administrative staff, and a class of students. Data were collected through observations, interviews, and documentation, and were analyzed using the Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña model through data condensation, data presentation, and conclusion drawing and verification, with data validity strengthened through cross-checking across sources and techniques. The findings show that teachers enhance learning motivation through systematic instructional planning, including the preparation of teaching modules, engaging learning activities, comprehensive assessment strategies, and adaptation of teaching methods to students’ characteristics. During implementation, teachers create a positive learning atmosphere through educational games, quizzes, discussions, question-and-answer sessions, group work, rewards, contextualization of learning materials, and regular content reviews. These efforts contribute to increased student participation, improved understanding of Islamic Religious Education materials, and the development of religious attitudes and character. The study recommends that teachers maintain varied and adaptive instructional strategies while strengthening students’ intrinsic motivation through meaningful learning experiences, positive reinforcement, role modeling, and collaboration between schools and parents.

items.title: Beyond the Evidence Coherence Trap: Agent-Driven Evidence Selection for Temporally Disordered Fake News Detection
items.abstract: Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. DelSA outperforms existing methods on ChronoFake, while remaining competitive on PolitiFact and GossipCop.

items.title: Bibliometric analysis of aviation unsafe event research: from reactive response to intelligent prediction
items.abstract: Purpose The post-pandemic recovery of global air transport and rapid developments in artificial intelligence are shifting aviation safety management from reactive accident investigation to proactive risk prediction. To examine how this trend is reflected in recent literature, this study aims to conduct a bibliometric analysis of aviation unsafe event research published between 2020 and 2025. Design/methodology/approach Based on 512 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, the authors use Bibliometrix and VOSviewer to construct keyword co-occurrence and co-citation networks. Findings The results show a rapid increase in research output following a temporary decline in 2022, reflecting the field’s resilience and growing attention to post-pandemic safety challenges. Thematic evolution analysis identifies a clear departure from traditional system-level investigations. This field increasingly prioritizes mining valuable information from flight data and unstructured safety reports using machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing. Current studies largely revolve around anomaly detection under complex meteorological conditions, causal inference using Bayesian networks and the application of large language models for safety text analysis. Originality/value These findings suggest that data-driven approaches have established themselves in aviation unsafe event research. Future studies should focus on addressing the interpretability of deep learning models and optimizing human–machine collaboration in safety-critical systems.

items.title: Biomedical Self-Supervised Learning using Sequential and Action-Conditioned Prediction: A Proof of Concept in Histopathology
items.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models for biomedical imaging are typically trained with non-sequential objectives that encourage invariance between augmented crops or predict missing content within a limited spatial resolution or range. This paradigm can be limiting for biomedical images, where diagnostically relevant structure often depends on relationships across widely different spatial extents and resolutions. We investigate sequential, action-conditioned prediction as an alternative self-supervised pretraining objective for biomedical imaging. As a proof of concept, we adapt seq-JEPA, originally developed for natural images, to 256 × 256 px histopathology images by extending its action space with zoom, and introduce seq-JEPA-dense, which predicts the next representation for every step in the sequence. Under the same per-crop augmentation distribution and with one run per method, seq-JEPA-dense improved tissue classification accuracy in the aggregated linear-probe evaluation from 88.3% to 91.9%, narrowing the gap to SimCLR, which achieved 93.3%. Both sequential variants recover a held-out crop from the preceding crops and the relative action leading to it at roughly twice the chance rate within the same image, indicating that the prediction depends on the action; whether position, zoom, or both drive this remains to be isolated. These results provide proof-of-concept evidence that sequential, action-conditioned self-supervision can be adapted to histopathology by extending its action space with zoom, yielding representations that approach a contrastive baseline, a first step toward its investigation as a self-supervised approach for extended biomedical images such as whole-slide images.

items.title: Bioprinting in Orthodontics: From Tissue Engineering to Personalized Regenerative Medicine
items.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting has emerged as an enabling technology in regenerative medicine with the potential to redefine the future of orthodontic treatment. By integrating living cells, biomaterials, and bioactive molecules through layer-by-layer fabrication, bioprinting enables the development of patient-specific constructs that closely replicate native craniofacial tissues. In orthodontics, this technology offers potential solutions for challenges such as alveolar bone deficiency, periodontal tissue loss, root resorption, craniofacial defects, and compromised tissue healing following orthodontic interventions. Recent advances in stem cell biology, bioactive hydrogels, tissue engineering, growth factor delivery, and digital manufacturing have expanded the scope of regenerative orthodontics beyond conventional biomechanical tooth movement. The incorporation of artificial intelligence, computer-aided design, cone-beam computed tomography, and additive manufacturing further supports precision treatment planning and customized regenerative therapies. Despite encouraging experimental outcomes, routine clinical implementation remains limited by challenges related to vascularization, scaffold maturation, manufacturing standardization, regulatory approval, long-term safety, and economic feasibility. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration among orthodontists, bioengineers, material scientists, and regulatory authorities is essential to translate laboratory innovations into predictable clinical applications. This article reviews the biological principles, technological advancements, clinical applications, translational challenges, and future perspectives of bioprinting, highlighting current evidence, existing limitations, and research priorities toward clinical translation.

items.title: Blockchain for space cybersecurity
items.abstract: Space infrastructure underpins modern civilisation but remains vulnerable because satellite communications, telemetry, and command systems rely heavily on centralised security architectures. As space becomes increasingly congested, contested, and commercialised, these architectures face growing threats from nation-state adversaries, cybercriminals, and supply chain compromise. This chapter examines blockchain technology as a structural countermeasure, highlighting how decentralisation, immutability, transparency, auditability, and trustless authentication address critical vulnerabilities across ground, space, user, cloud, communication, and supply chain segments. A permissioned consortium blockchain model is proposed to balance resilience, operational confidentiality, and national sovereignty requirements. The chapter explores blockchain-enabled applications including tamper-evident audit trails, decentralised identity and access management, distributed threat detection, smart contract governance, space situational awareness, autonomous satellite operations, and secure inter-satellite communications. It also analyses deployment challenges and future research directions involving post-quantum cryptography, Zero Trust Architecture, AI-enhanced smart contracts, and cislunar blockchain ecosystems for resilient and trustworthy next-generation space cybersecurity frameworks worldwide.

items.title: Body mass index modifies the noise-hypertension link: a cross-sectional study in automobile workers
items.abstract: Background Occupational noise is a pervasive occupational hazard. While it is a well-established cause of hearing loss, only a few studies have suggested a potential association with cardiovascular diseases, and the evidence remains limited. Furthermore, individual susceptibility varies substantially, and metabolic characteristics, such as body mass index (BMI), may play a modifying role. Objective To systematically examine the effect of BMI modification on occupational noise exposure duration and hypertension risk. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among workers at an automobile manufacturing plant. Demographics, occupational history, and medical examinations were collected. Modified Poisson regression models were used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs). The modifying effect of continuous BMI was evaluated by incorporating an interaction term, with a sensitivity analysis performed using binary BMI classifications. Johnson-Neyman technique was used to determine the point at which the association was no longer statistically significant. Results There were 21.6% of participants with hypertension in this plant. Occupational noise exposure duration was positively associated with the risk of hypertension. The continuous BMI showed a significant negative interaction with noise exposure duration (PR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.979–0.995], P = 0.001). Specifically, at a BMI of 18.5 kg/m 2 , each additional year of noise exposure duration increased hypertension risk by 11.9% (PR = 1.119, 95% CI [1.047–1.196]); at a BMI of 24.0 kg/m 2 , this association was attenuated but remained significant (PR = 1.041, 95% CI [1.008–1.075]); and at a BMI of 28.0 kg/m 2 , no significant association was observed (PR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.956–1.019]). With Johnson–Neyman, the BMI value above which the estimated association was no longer statistically significant was identified at 27.02 kg/m 2 . In sensitivity analysis, treating BMI as a binary variable, the association between noise exposure duration and hypertension risk was attenuated and no longer statistically significant in overweight/obese individuals but remained significant in normal-weight individuals, and the negative interaction between noise exposure duration and BMI remained statistically significant (PR = 0.919, 95% CI [0.863–0.979], P = 0.010). Conclusions The association between occupational noise exposure duration and hypertension risk was modified by BMI in this cross-sectional study of automobile manufacturing workers. The association was more pronounced among normal-weight workers, whereas it was attenuated and no longer statistically significant at higher BMI levels. These findings suggest that BMI may be an important consideration in occupational health surveillance and hypertension risk assessment among noise-exposed workers, warranting further longitudinal investigation.

items.title: Bootstrap Stability and Learner Sensitivity in Bayesian Network Modeling of near Midair Collision Incidents Using Aviation Safety Narratives and Operational Data
items.abstract: Near midair collisions (NMACs) remain a complex aviation safety challenge shaped by operational conditions and human factors. Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) narratives provide useful information about communication, visual acquisition, workload, and other event circumstances, but relationships identified from voluntary reports may vary across analytical approaches and over time. This study examined 13,111 NMAC-related ASRS reports from 1988 to 2025 to identify stable report-level associations among operational conditions, encounter proximity, narrative topics, and reported evasive action. Across two Bayesian-network approaches and 500 paired bootstrap samples, traffic-pattern operations/training and tower communication/sequencing were the strongest variables directly associated with reported evasive action. Their recurrence was moderate rather than universal, however, and their inclusion changed under different relationship-selection thresholds. This indicates that the local structure around reported evasive action was sensitive to modeling decisions, even though the two variables consistently ranked as the leading response-adjacent candidates. Additional robustness checks preserved these two response parents in the full-data models while showing changes in the broader network structure. A temporal evaluation produced a different pattern. Models trained on reports from 1988 to 2019 and evaluated on reports from 2020 to 2025 instead identified airspace structure/radar-contact issues and final-approach/base-to-final conflicts as the response-adjacent variables. Because the narrative-topic features were derived from the full corpus, this analysis represents a temporal evaluation conditional on a fixed topic representation, rather than a fully independent validation of the complete modeling pipeline. The changed response parents therefore indicate temporal sensitivity but do not establish nonstationarity. The findings describe associations within voluntary safety reports and should not be interpreted as evidence of causality, collision risk, or operational warning performance. The study contributes a reproducible, systematically stress-tested framework for evaluating Bayesian-network findings in aviation safety narratives. It identifies communication, sequencing, visual acquisition, and traffic-pattern operations as priorities for expert review and prospective measurement while cautioning against treating relationships found in historical narratives as stable operational predictors.

items.title: Brain-Inspired AI in Industry, Infrastructure, and Innovation
items.abstract: The accelerating integration of brain-inspired artificial intelligence into industrial systems marks a transformative moment for sustainable engineering, directly advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 9 on Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure. This chapter provides a rigorous, engineering-oriented examination of how neuroscience principles, including spike-timing-dependent plasticity, predictive coding, hierarchical sensory processing, and lateral inhibition, are being systematically translated into industrial AI architectures with compelling real-world impact. Six interconnected domains are explored: cognitive robotics and human–machine collaboration using ACT-R-grounded spiking neural networks; digital twin-integrated predictive maintenance leveraging liquid state machines and event-driven spike encoding; energy-aware neuromorphic computing for sustainable manufacturing, achieving up to 10,000× power reduction over GPU-based systems; brain-inspired hierarchical decision systems and neuro-symbolic integration for explainable smart factory control; ethical workforce transition frameworks addressing automation’s socioeconomic implications; and six global innovation case studies spanning wind turbine health monitoring, electric vehicle battery assembly, smart city traffic optimization, and predictive water infrastructure management. Collectively, these applications demonstrate that brain-inspired AI is not merely a technical advancement but a principled pathway toward more resilient, equitable, and environmentally sustainable industrial systems aligned with international development goals.

items.title: Bridging Human–AI Interaction and Human–Robot Interaction: Shared Challenges, Converging Futures
items.abstract: This panel examines the growing convergence of human–AI interaction (HAI) and human–robot interaction (HRI) as intelligent systems become more autonomous, embodied, and embedded in everyday settings such as healthcare, education, homes, and workplaces. Although HAI and HRI have evolved as distinct fields, the panel argues that shared human factors concerns—such as trust, safety, autonomy, teamwork, situation awareness, evaluation, and responsible deployment—now require greater integration across both domains. Drawing on perspectives from leading researchers and doctoral students, the session explores how embodiment, motion, social cues, and system transparency shape human interaction with AI and robots. It also addresses methodological tensions, including laboratory versus field evaluation and short-term versus longitudinal study, while highlighting implications for ethics, training, and design. Overall, the panel aims to identify common challenges, foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, and outline a research roadmap for human-centered intelligent systems that improve performance, well-being, and quality of life across diverse contexts and sectors.

items.title: Calibrated agents as market makers: automated liquidity provision for long-tail prediction markets
items.abstract: Abstract Under what conditions can a forecasting agent profitably provide liquidity on a prediction market? We derive a decomposition of the optimal market-making spread into a microstructure term and an adverse selection term proportional to the agent's mean absolute estimation error~$\alpha$. The profitability condition $s > 2\varphi\alpha$ depends only on the sign of per-fill profit and holds for any positive fill-rate function. A threshold theorem shows that tolerable calibration error increases with existing market spread---a comparative static suggesting that calibrated agents may add the most value on illiquid long-tail markets that lack human market makers. Monte Carlo simulations across 3{,}000 synthetic markets calibrated to empirical Polymarket parameters ($\kappa = 36$) show win rates near 68--70\% across calibration levels, with mean profit varying by $3.4\times$ (\$5.83 to \$1.72), confirming that calibration quality drives profit magnitude. On the empirical side, the main finding is a calibration gap: five frontier LLMs evaluated on 15 resolved Polymarket questions reveal that market-alignment error (MAD $\leq$ 0.029) underestimates true estimation error ($\alpha$ up to 0.437) by an order of magnitude---a result with implications for any system using market prices as calibration targets. The model omits inventory risk and multi-agent competition, limiting direct deployment conclusions, but the spread decomposition provides a tractable framework for analyzing when AI-agent liquidity provision is viable. items.title: CaLLM: Continual Adaptation of LLMs via Non-Parametric Adapter Routing
items.abstract: Continual adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to evolving task distributions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting remains an open problem. Existing strategies often struggle to scale or lack a robust mechanism for zero-shot task-to-expert assignment. We introduce CaLLM, a framework that resolves these tensions by combining metric-based meta-learning with modular parameter isolation via lightweight adapters. First, CaLLM projects each input batch into a task-agnostic embedding space to find its nearest prototype. It then routes the batch to the specific adapter specialized for that data distribution. This formulation provides (i)~controllable cross-task interference by design, (ii)~constant computational complexity regardless of task count, (iii)~seamless integration of novel distributions through prototype expansion, and (iv)~regime agnosticism as the local routing decision enables a unified approach to both online and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that this routing mechanism discovers semantically coherent task groupings while facilitating constructive interference between similar tasks, and keeping overhead at a minimum. Across diverse and fine-grained continual learning benchmarks, CaLLM consistently outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods, establishing prototype-based modular routing as a principled and scalable approach to lifelong adaptation of LLMs.

items.title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.

items.title: Can Large Language Models Judge Stroke Information on Social Media? A Cross-Sectional Comparison of Large Language Models Against Human Ratings of Health-Related Videos
items.abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) reproduce human assessments of the quality of stroke-related information on social media. Background Social media is a major source of health information, yet content quality varies. The reliability of LLMs in evaluating stroke-related social media content against human assessments remains uncertain. Methods This cross-sectional study evaluated 50 TikTok and Instagram videos using human reference scores and three AI models: ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Claude. Publicly unavailable videos and those featuring songs or lacking transcribable speech were excluded. Spoken audio was transcribed using a free tool, and transcripts were submitted to all three models with an identical standardized prompt. Scores were compared using Mann–Whitney U tests; Spearman’s correlation assessed associations with human ratings, and linear regression quantified explained variance. Results The median human reference score was 37.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00). All AI models scored significantly lower: ChatGPT, 34.50 (p = 0.001); Microsoft Copilot, 33.50 (p < 0.001); and Claude, 26.00 (p < 0.001). All models correlated significantly with human ratings, with the strongest association for Claude (ρ = 0.593; p < 0.001), followed by ChatGPT (ρ = 0.550; p < 0.001) and Copilot (ρ = 0.396; p = 0.004). Claude explained 32.1% of the variance in human scores (R² = 0.321), compared with 31.4% for ChatGPT and 14.8% for Copilot. Inter-model correlation was strongest between ChatGPT and Copilot (ρ = 0.862; p < 0.001). Conclusions All three LLMs showed significant positive correlations with human ratings but systematically assigned lower scores. Claude showed the strongest correlation, whereas Microsoft Copilot showed the weakest. These findings highlight the limitations of LLMs in reproducing human judgments and the need for further validation before their use as standalone evaluators of social media content.

items.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.

items.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
items.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

items.title: Can routine chest CT with artificial intelligence tool be used for opportunistically osteoporosis screening? A preliminary study
items.abstract: Introduction Patients with pulmonary diseases face an elevated risk of osteoporosis. Conventional diagnosis relies on quantitative computed tomography (QCT), which delivers a high radiation dose and requires a dedicated scan. Whether conventional chest CT can be used for osteoporosis screening remains uncertain. Methods A deep learning system was used to measure bone mineral density (BMD) in routine chest CT scans for osteoporosis screening, with QCT as the reference standard. A total of 98 patients who underwent chest and abdominal CT due to medical conditions between August 2024 and March 2025 were analyzed. The BMD of the thoracic vertebrae (T1-T12) was measured, three consecutive vertebral bodies were grouped into averages, and the results were compared with the BMD of the lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) measured by standard QCT. The differences and agreement between the two BMD measurement methods were compared, and the diagnostic performance for osteoporosis and low bone mass was assessed by receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Results The cohort included 98 patients (48 female, 50 male; mean age 49.48 ± 14.64 years). AI-measured thoracic vertebrae BMD correlated highly with QCT BMD (r: 0.72-0.92), with the highest correlation observed for T10-T12 (r = 0.98, P < 0.001). All AI-BMD measurements demonstrated high diagnostic performance for osteoporosis and low bone mass. In the osteoporosis analysis,the T10-T12 BMD achieved the highest AUC of 0.998 (95% CI: 0.960-1.000), with an optimal diagnostic threshold of BMD ≤90.86 mg/cm³ (sensitivity 100.0%, specificity 97.6%). In the low-bone-mass analysis, the AUC was 0.990 (95% CI: 0.945-1.000). The volumetric CT dose index for QCT scans was significantly higher than that for chest CT scans (14.63 ± 2.30 vs. 4.13 ± 1.01 mGy, P < 0.001), and the post-processing time for QCT was significantly longer than that for the AI-based measurement (55.76 ± 9.05 vs. 7.50 ± 0.78 s, P < 0.001). Conclusion AI-based BMD measurements from chest CT correlate highly with QCT measurements. AI-derived thoracic BMD from routine chest CT may serve as a potential opportunistic screening-support tool for osteoporosis and low bone mass, but further validation in larger, multicenter, prospective cohorts is required before clinical adoption.

items.title: Cannula detachment during intraocular surgery: Impact, implications and what the theatre team can do
items.abstract: Cannula detachment during intraocular surgery is an uncommon but potentially blinding complication. When it happens, attention commonly turns to whether the scrub practitioner tightened the connection adequately. This article explains why a well-made connection can still fail under hydraulic load once the junction has been lubricated, why incomplete tightening, where it occurs, is better understood as a foreseeable human factor than as an individual failing, why the cause cannot be established from the outcome alone and what theatre teams can do to reduce the risk and limit the harm.

items.title: Capability-Adaptive Intelligent Assistance in Industry 5.0 Manufacturing: A Systematic Review and Research Framework
items.abstract: Abstract Industry 5.0 reframes manufacturing around human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience, and a growing literature has developed intelligent assistance systems human-robot collaboration, AI-driven perception, digital twins, and extended-reality interfaces in pursuit of this aim. Whether this literature accommodates the heterogeneity of the workers it aims to center has not been systematically established. This review analyzes 14,346 Web of Science records (2016–2026, screened from 15,038 raw records across 19 export files, using an empirically validated Advanced Search query) addressing Industry 5.0 manufacturing. Bibliometric analysis confirms a technology-dominant field: robotics/cobots and AI/ML content appear in 51.9% and 26.8% of records respectively, while human-factors and interaction-modality content appear in 11.6% and 10.0%. A purposively verified subsample of 62 records 19 disability-explicit, 8 age-explicit, 4 cognitive/neurodiversity-explicit, and 31 addressing digital literacy or general capability accommodation was identified and hand-checked against the full corpus; despite this real and previously undercounted body of work, capability-diversity terms remain essentially absent from the field's dominant keyword co-occurrence structure (fewer than 3 co-occurrences for any disability-related pair, against 425 for the corpus's leading pair). This indicates a literature that exists but has not been synthesized, is rarely cross-cited, and remains disconnected from the mainstream human-centric Industry 5.0 discourse and its dominant AI-driven technology stack. We propose the Capability-Adaptive Intelligent Assistance Framework for Industry 5.0 (CAIA-5.0), connecting this scattered capability-accommodation literature to current AI-driven assistance mechanisms, with one extension profile-conditioned autonomy allocation explicitly flagged as untested. A six-item research agenda specifies the empirical, technological, and synthesis work required to connect this fragmented literature into a coherent, industrially applicable framework. The review offers manufacturing system designers, human-factors engineers, and policymakers a diagnostic basis and implementation roadmap for inclusive intelligent assistance.

items.title: Case Study: Pacific Heights University Gambling
items.abstract: Abstract This case study examines the downfall of Pacific Heights University’s celebrated president, Dr. Samuel Whitaker, whose hidden gambling addiction led to the misappropriation of university funds and plunged the institution into crisis. Through detailed narrative and multi-perspective analysis, the study explores the interplay between personal vulnerability and organizational oversight in higher education. It traces Whitaker’s rise as a turnaround leader, his gradual descent into addiction, the discovery of financial misconduct, and the university’s efforts to restore trust and implement meaningful reforms. By synthesizing the institutional, personal, and societal dimensions of the crisis, the case offers vital lessons on ethical leadership, the necessity of robust controls, and the human factors that can undermine even the most trusted administrators. The narrative concludes with a unified reflection on recovery, accountability, and the enduring importance of vigilance in safeguarding institutional integrity.

items.title: Cataract Surgery in Patients Unable to Lie Flat: A Systematic Review and Surgical Decision-Making Framework
items.abstract: PURPOSE: To systematically review all described approaches to cataract surgery in patients unable to lie supine and propose a clinical decision-making framework. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Conditions precluding supine positioning include kyphosis, orthopnoea, and morbid obesity, which affect a substantial and growing proportion of patients requiring cataract surgery. No standardised guidance exists to direct surgical management in this population, representing a meaningful gap given that cataract surgery is the most cost-effective operation in medicine. METHODS: This systematic review underwent prospective PROSPERO registration (CRD420261288661). In accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically searched and appraised all described approaches to completed cataract surgery in patients unable to recline for any reason across PubMed, Scopus, and EMBase on August 25th, 2025. Data were extracted regarding technique, equipment required, ergonomic considerations for surgeon and patient, and secondary outcomes including complications or position-specific challenges. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale for case-control and cohort studies, and the Murad Tool for case series and case reports. RESULTS: Twenty-five studies were included, demonstrating three dominant approaches that have been utilized to perform cataract surgery in patients unable to lie supine: special positioning to facilitate a semi-recumbent position, surgery carried out with the surgeon standing, and positioning so that the surgeon and patient are face-to-face during surgery. There are only a few instances where conventional phacoemulsification has been performed under slit lamp microscopy in seated patients, presenting only limited data evaluating the safety of this practice. CONCLUSIONS: There are three distinct categories of approaching cataract surgery on patients unable to recline, which although still technically challenging, can increase the number of patients eligible to undergo cataract surgery in both developed and developing countries. We present a clinical decision framework proposed to guide approach selection based on mechanism of positional limitation, equipment availability, and case complexity.

items.title: Changes in Perceptions of Trust in Human-AI Interactions
items.abstract: This study examined how educational briefings about Artificial Intelligence (AI) hallucinations influence user trust, caution, and willingness to continue using AI systems. We recruited 51 participants through the online platform Prolific for an online questionnaire evaluating AI use and task-focused AI scenarios. After questions about trust and AI, participants read about common inaccuracies in Large Language Models. Participants showed a significant decrease in self-reported trust, indicating increased awareness of AI limitations. Contrary to expectations, perceptions of AI reliability and competence did not predict willingness to reuse AI in academic scenarios. Affective trust played a stronger role than cognitive trust, with perceived emotional support significantly predicting forgiveness of AI errors. Increased caution also predicted greater recalibration of trust, although willingness to continue using AI remained high. These findings suggest that educational interventions can promote calibrated trust in AI without discouraging continued use, highlighting the importance of transparency and context-sensitive design.

items.title: Cheap First, Ask the LLM Later? Cost and Accuracy of Rule-Based, Native-PDF, and Text-Based LLM Extraction of Syllabus Deadlines
items.abstract: Students receive assessment deadlines inside course syllabi, usually as PDFs, and a growing number of tools use large language models (LLMs) to turn these documents into calendars. A common cost-saving design runs cheap rules first and calls the LLM only when the rules appear to fail. We test whether this saves money without losing accuracy. We compare five strategies on 16 public syllabi from eight institutions (151 hand-verified deadlines): regular-expression rules, a general-purpose date library, an LLM given the native PDF, an LLM given text extracted from the PDF, and a rule-first hybrid that calls the LLM only when the rules find fewer than three events. Each LLM strategy was run three times with gemini-3.1-flash-lite. The LLM strategies reached F1 scores of 0.708 (native PDF) and 0.657 (extracted text); the difference was not significant (p = 0.13), and the native-PDF input used fewer tokens with this model. The rule-first hybrid used 57.8% fewer tokens than the text-based LLM but lowered F1 to 0.370, a significant loss (p = 0.002). Rules alone scored 0.186, and 58% of their correctly placed month-day matches carried the wrong year. A sweep of the hybrid's routing threshold shows that every token saved cost accuracy. We release the code, labels, and all predictions.

items.title: Closed-loop cognitive state control: a hypothesis framework for real-time estimation, stabilization, and recovery of task-specific high-performance cognitive states
items.abstract: Human performance often fails not because latent capacity is absent, but because access to high-functioning cognitive states is unstable under fatigue, distraction, overload, and pressure. This hypothesis paper proposes closed-loop cognitive state control—informally, supercognition —as a neuroengineering objective: rapid entry into, stabilization of, and recovery of an individual's highest available task-specific cognitive state. The framework treats cognition as a partially observable dynamical system whose latent states would be inferred from multimodal behavioral, physiological, contextual, and neural signals, and specifies a five-layer architecture comprising multimodal sensing, latent-state inference, predictive transition modeling, closed-loop intervention, and a longitudinal personal neural twin. The proposal is situated against existing closed-loop and neuroadaptive architectures, with an explicit statement of what is and is not new. The state ontology is given as a set of falsifiable assumptions rather than an intuitive taxonomy. Candidate computational implementations are specified for each layer, including hidden semi-Markov and switching state-space models, Bayesian and Kalman filtering, sequence models, hazard models, contextual bandits, model-predictive control, and offline reinforcement learning. The personal neural twin receives an operational specification covering its data requirements, update schedule, calibration and drift-monitoring criteria, and failure modes. Predictive and causal claims are separated, with the evidentiary requirements stated for each. The paper engages directly with the literature that challenges the framework's feasibility, including biomarker reliability, mixed neurofeedback findings, cross-task and cross-subject generalization failure, and the ecological-validity gap in wearable neurotechnology. Operational definitions, application scenarios, a validation protocol with power and diversity requirements, an expanded ethics and governance analysis, and a staged research roadmap are provided. No component of the architecture has been implemented or evaluated here: no simulation, clinical trial, or empirical efficacy claim is presented, and the validation programme described is prospective. The contribution is a falsifiable systems-engineering hypothesis for cognitive-state control.

items.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments
items.abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.

items.title: CoHARL: Co-Evolving Agent Policies and Executable Harnesses with Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through executable harnesses that govern tool use and feedback. Optimizing a harness for a fixed policy overlooks how its behavior changes during learning, while training a policy under a fixed harness leaves the interface that generates its training experience unchanged. This motivates adapting the harness throughout policy training. We introduce CoHARL, a population-based reinforcement learning framework that co-evolves a shared policy and a population of executable harnesses. The policy learns from rollouts across the population, and a proposer uses its execution traces to revise harness code during training. CoHARL achieves a 27.6% mean resolved rate on SWE-rebench, improving over harness-only search by 6.4 percentage points. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show gains in software engineering and terminal-based tasks. Under matched training budgets, CoHARL also outperforms searching for a harness once before RL and alternating policy updates with revisions to a single active harness.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Rule-Based, Deep Learning, and LLM Approaches for Causality Extraction: A Unified Benchmark
items.abstract: Abstract Causality extraction—the identification of cause–effect relations in natural language text—has been approached through three successive methodological paradigms: rule-based systems relying on lexical and syntactic cues, deep learning models exploiting neural architectures and pre-trained encoders, and, most recently, large language models (LLMs) applied through prompting or fine-tuning. Each paradigm has been evaluated on different datasets, under different annotation schemes, and with different metrics, making it difficult to determine how far apparent performance differences reflect genuine methodological advantages rather than benchmark artifacts. This study addresses that problem by constructing a unified benchmark for comparative evaluation of rule-based, deep learning, and LLM approaches to causality extraction. We consolidate multiple existing corpora—covering news, biomedical, and safety-incident text—into a harmonized annotation format, re-annotate a stratified subset to ensure consistent treatment of implicit and explicit causal relations, and evaluate representative methods from each paradigm under identical preprocessing, train–test splits, and evaluation protocols. We report span-level precision, recall, and F1, document-level F1, calibration error, inference cost, and annotation efficiency, and we conduct cross-domain transfer experiments to assess generalization. Results are analyzed to disentangle the contributions of architecture, training data, and task formulation, with particular attention to the conditions under which each paradigm retains a comparative advantage. We further examine error profiles across paradigms, identifying whether failures are concentrated in explicit versus implicit relations, local versus distributed constructions, and domain-specific versus general-language contexts.

items.title: Competence narrowing in AI-assisted oral English instruction: A quasi-experimental study of the spiral synergy framework
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative AI tools into spoken English instruction has produced measurable fluency and accuracy gains, but whether these are evenly distributed across the dimensions of communicative competence remains underexplored. This quasi-experimental study compares the Spiral Synergy Framework (SSF), a three-layer pedagogical sequence (AI Consolidation, Bridging Tasks, Interpersonal Activation), against conventional AI-integrated instruction in two intact Business English classes at a Chinese higher vocational college (experimental n = 36, control n = 34), using oral recordings at three time points scored on five competence dimensions, 15 weeks of classroom observation, and an intra-rater reliability check. The two classes differed significantly at baseline on the oral composite score and three of five dimensions (control higher), though not on CET-4 proficiency or questionnaire items. Because treatment is confounded with class membership and both classes received AI-assisted practice, findings are reported as associations rather than demonstrated causal effects. Linear mixed-effects models testing Group × Time interactions across five outcomes (four dimensions and the composite), corrected for multiple comparisons, identified one outcome - real-time responsiveness - on which the classes diverged: the experimental class maintained responsiveness across the semester while the control class declined despite its baseline advantage (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = .029), a result that held under a cluster-robust sensitivity check. No corrected between-group difference was found for improvisation, coherence, naturalness, or the composite score; improvisation declined descriptively in both classes over the semester. Classroom observation data (experimental class only) document a recurring, non-monotonic cycle of AI-dependency reduction and rebound across 15 weeks. Intra-rater test-retest reliability of the oral-competence ratings was moderate to good (ICC = .67-.91), though this reflects a single rater familiar with participants rather than independent inter-rater agreement. Implications for multidimensional assessment, task sequencing, and cautious interpretation of AI-integrated curriculum research are discussed.

items.title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

items.title: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, a task's primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward: on a failing response, an auxiliary cannot exceed the primary. However, group-relative advantage estimators treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, so it can reverse the primary's order, and at the primary's ceiling only auxiliaries order responses. Keeping gated auxiliaries hurts some tasks, while dropping them hurts others. We propose CONCUR, an advantage estimator that replaces the standardized scores of each gated auxiliary with the closest scores that satisfy two conditions: responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores, and responses at the primary's ceiling receive equal scores. CONCUR-T applies both conditions throughout training, and CONCUR-A lifts the second for an auxiliary that agrees with the primary's order more often than it reverses it among passing responses. On three models from two families and across math, code, instruction following, and writing, both variants score higher on average than all baselines and than when all the gated auxiliaries are dropped.

items.title: Conditional Values: The Contingent Foundations of Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: How do broader values shape whether people judge artificial intelligence (AI) as good or bad for humanity? This article analyzes provisional World Values Survey Wave 8 data from 40,960 respondents in 24 country samples using pooled and national prediction models, outcome-independent respondent profiles, and groups of countries. The analysis reveals a cross-country anchor: general optimism about science and technology is the strongest pooled predictor of favorable AI evaluation and recurs among the leading predictors in every national sample. Expert authority, education and information access, selected forms of trust, openness, and demographic position provide nationally distinctive patterns. Eleven value profiles formed without AI attitudes span 49.1% to 62.2% favorable evaluation. Most evaluative variation occurs within these profiles, making them useful contexts for identifying how the same values distinguish favorable from unfavorable evaluators in different social configurations. Institutional legitimacy, structural advantage, information connectedness, personal choice, redistribution, and openness differentiate evaluations in particular profiles. The same axis can relate differently to AI evaluation across profiles: secular reasoning has a significant positive association among secular moderate pluralists but a suggestive negative association among institution-trusting civic joiners. Together, the findings show that public receptivity to AI as technological change has a common predictive anchor but develops within plural configurations of resources, institutions, authority, openness, and social position. This distinction helps anticipate where generalized technological optimism is likely to travel and where AI deployment and governance will encounter context-specific sources of legitimacy or concern.

items.title: ConfluxServe: Reconciling Resource Utilization and Parallelism Efficiency across Prefill and Decode in LLM Serving
items.abstract: Prefill and decode are complementary in resource usage, but often divergent in parallelism preferences. Executing the two phases separately preserves their preferred parallelism but leaves complementary resources underutilized, while co-batching improves utilization but often requires a uniform parallel configuration that hurts execution efficiency. To resolve this utilization-efficiency dilemma, we propose Conflux Parallelism (XP), a parallel execution abstraction that co-executes prefill and decode with different parallelism within the same batch. Conflux Parallelism exploits operator-level Transformer structure to construct a heterogeneous execution path with different batching and parallelism strategies across operators, combining the best of co-batching and phase-specific execution. Building on Conflux Parallelism, we design ConfluxServe, an SLO-aware serving system that maximizes cluster goodput under TTFT and TBT constraints. Evaluation on production workloads shows that ConfluxServe improves serving goodput by 1.26-1.62x over the strongest baselines.

items.title: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure
items.abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. items.title: Coverage Under Contradiction: A Benchmark for Negation-Aware Retrieval
items.abstract: Coverage-evaluation benchmarks quantify whether retrieved evidence covers the different pieces of information needed to satisfy an information need. Existing benchmarks mostly consider factual claims that may already be known to pretrained retrieval components, leaving open whether retrievers find corpus evidence when it contradicts those priors. We study how retrievers behave when their parametric knowledge and the information in a corpus disagree. To do so, we develop a process to augment a nugget-based coverage benchmark with controlled contradictions. For each nugget, we create a negated counterpart and edit its supporting documents to support that negation while preserving the context. Applying this process to CoverageBench, a benchmark measuring information coverage, we create CoverageBench-Negate, spanning six datasets and roughly 63,000 original-edited evidence pairs (one per nugget-document link). We attach rich construction metadata to every pair and additionally provide out-of-family LLM judgments over all pairs and a human audit of a sample. In baseline experiments, BM25 separates original from edited near-twin evidence substantially better than dense retrievers (Qwen3 and Jina), which stay near chance. We release the benchmark on Hugging Face Datasets (nuggets, documents, pairs) together with the construction materials, including the prompts used to create it.
