items.title: From Proposal to Discovery: Attribution, Validation, and Responsibility in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Science / De la propuesta al descubrimiento: atribución, validación y responsabilidad en la ciencia asistida por inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: ENGLISH This critical conceptual essay examines how to distinguish a proposed AI-assisted scientific discovery from its validation, the documented contributions of participants, and responsibility for communicating the result. It develops a four-register framework covering the scientific claim, the standard of evidence attained, the provenance of contributions, and communication responsibility. Published examples illustrate why generating hypotheses or computational results is not, by itself, equivalent to validating all claims made about them. The essay reports no original experiment or systematic review; the proposed framework has not been empirically validated. This record contains the complete English and Spanish editions, Version 1.0. items.title: From Ripple to Boundary: Deterministic Impact Boundaries for LLM-Based Software Evolution
items.abstract: The landscape of software evolution is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift in the era of Large Language Models. As industrial software engineering increasingly transitions toward design-driven code generation, the bottleneck of evolution has shifted from writing code to maintaining deterministic consistency between multi-source design assets and the generated code. When a design asset changes, LLM agents currently lack a deterministic impact boundary to identify which code must be evolved, leading to two failure modes: hallucinating missing changes or breaking unrelated code. Probabilistic approaches, such as semantic retrieval or text-based diffing, fail to capture the structural ripple effects across highly interconnected design dependencies. We propose a paradigm shift from probabilistic semantic retrieval to deterministic structural constraints. We formalize the design assets as a Knowledge Graph and organize them into a content-addressed Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph. Our key insight reveals a topological isomorphism between the logical ripple effect of a design change and the content hash propagation within the DAG. By leveraging this, we transform ambiguous impact analysis into verifiable structural operations. Through a two-phase diffing process, we extract a precise causal chain that defines the exact modification boundary. This boundary enables deterministic context injection, providing the LLM agent with strictly scoped code and design updates, thereby fundamentally guaranteeing evolution safety. As a by-product, the KG serves as an agent-queryable knowledge base for natural language design retrieval. Early deployment on a large-scale industrial payment platform demonstrates that our mechanism successfully computes the exact impact boundary and generates incremental code modifications that meet the expected design changes.

items.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.

items.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. items.title: GarmentSegAgent: Autonomous Garment Segmentation for Web Fashion Images via Textual Self-Refinement
items.abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.

items.title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.
